newsitem.title: USA: McVeigh's lead attorney will withdraw from case.
newsitem.headline: McVeigh's lead attorney will withdraw from case.

text.p: Stephen Jones, Timothy McVeigh's lead attorney, said on Monday he would ask a court to let him stop representing the convicted Oklahoma City bomber.

Jones said he was acting because of an interview McVeigh gave the Buffalo (New York) News in which he said the attorney had "screwed up badly" in conducting his defense, lied to him and succceeded in getting him the death penalty.
"It's motivated by Mr. McVeigh's comments last week in the Buffalo News," Jones told Reuters in an telephone interview from his home in Enid, Oklahoma.
In June in Denver, McVeigh was convicted and sentenced to die for bombing the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City. The April 19, 1995, blast killed 168 people.
McVeigh's co-defendant and former Army buddy Terry Nichols is to go on trial on Sept. 29.
McVeigh's only hope now for avoiding the death penalty lies in a lengthy appeals process.

An appeals court official said last week that a court-appointed attorney in a federal trial automatically continued to represent a defendant on appeal unless the court accepted the attorney's request to withdraw.
"I hope to have it on file tomorrow" at the 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Denver, Jones said.
"I thought I should bring (his client's newspaper interview) to the attention of the court and ask them for permission to withdraw," he said.
Last week Jones said it would not be appropriate for him to respond to McVeigh's comments and he would continue to represent McVeigh unless judges removed him from the case.
It was disclosed last week that soon after jurors sentenced McVeigh to death, he wrote trial judge Richard Matsch of Federal District Court saying he had had "problems and difficulties" with Jones.
McVeigh did not elaborate on them until last week's newspaper interview.
Jones said on Monday he had not spoken with McVeigh after the interview, which appeared last Wednesday, one day before Matsch formally pronounced the death sentence.
